opening.headline: When old tool results take over context, learn how to decide whether to reduce them to a summary or clear them with a rule.
body: The coding agent receives tool results every time it opens a file, searches, or runs a test. The results once processed are reloaded with each request even dozens of times later, and the response quality begins to deteriorate even before the window fills up.

This lesson compares two approaches to reducing outdated content: compaction and context editing. We will look at examples of how setting the compression threshold affects quality and cost, and see how Claude, ADK, and OpenAI set the same principle.
opening.objectivesLead: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:
objectives: Can explain the difference between compaction and context editing
Analyze the impact of compression threshold settings on quality and cost

marks.note: This is the file content that has been read once and already processed. Even after dozens of turns, it continues to catch up and increase the input token for each request.
Long logs often require only a line or two of conclusion. If the original text remains, signals unrelated to the current request will fill the window.
This is a rule that really needs to be followed. As tool results accumulate, these key instructions become relatively buried.
What we need now is information related to this request. You should consider whether the rest can be summarized or deleted.

screens.outro: To solve this problem, you need to decide what to summarize and what to delete altogether. First, let me recall a similar experience.

screens.title: Think about it: the latter part of a longer work.
screens.lead: When you select each question, the instructor's thoughts unfold. You won't have to enter or submit your answer, so think about it in your head first and then press it.

items.prompt: Have you ever seen an agent lose track of initial requirements the longer they work?
items.answer: The longer the conversation goes on even before the window fills, the lower the quality of the response can be. This is because the initial requirements are buried in the content that piles up later. So we need to keep the active context small before passing the window.

items.prompt: Imagine that the long output returned by the tool continues to follow from the next turn.
items.answer: Tool results are often not needed again once the model has processed them, but they remain in the conversation history if no action is taken. Larger results, such as file content or search results, have a greater impact.

items.prompt: If you've ever tried to 'summarize and start over' a conversation, look back and see what you missed.
items.answer: Summary is necessarily lossy. It is easy to miss the reasons for the decision, unresolved problems, and detailed conditions stated by the user. An important theme of this lesson is that what you leave behind depends on how you summarize and your instructions.

screens.outro: Now that we've summarized our experience, let's compare two approaches to reducing.

screens.title: Two approaches: summarize or rule out
screens.lead: Select each tab to learn how compression and context editing work and the differences.

visual.alt: A two-line comparison schematic where Compress turns old turns into summaries and Context Edit turns tool results into placeholders.

tabs.label: Compression
tabs.body: Compaction reduces the actual content by replacing old turns with summaries written by the model on the server. The summary supersedes previous content, so tokens are significantly reduced while continuing the flow of conversation and decisions. Instead, details may get lost in the summary process.

tabs.label: Edit context
tabs.body: Context editing does not create a summary. Clear old tool results or thinking blocks according to your rules. A placeholder text indicating that the model has been deleted will remain where it has been deleted, letting you know that the model has been deleted. On the server side, prompts are applied before they hit the model, and the client retains the original conversation history.

tabs.label: common goal
tabs.body: The goal of both methods is the same. The goal is to keep the active context small to avoid quality degradation. The difference is the means. Compression is a summary that tries to preserve meaning, and editing removes unnecessary parts according to established rules.

tabs.label: Three compression methods
tabs.body: The Claude document divides compression methods into three types: There are three methods: an on-demand method that sets a point in time with a request, an API that executes at a threshold, and a client method that directly places a summarizer. If you have your own summarizer, all of the summarization calls, prompts, and rewriting of records will have to be handled by your code.

screens.outro: Now let's look at how compression is set, focusing on thresholds.

screens.title: Compaction and compression threshold
screens.lead: Read the settings below and check the meaning of each item and symptoms when the value is incorrectly set in the explanation on the right.

notes.note: To use compression you need to turn on the beta. If you do not turn it on, compression will not work even if you send the context_management setting.

Add strategy compact_20260112 to edits to turn on compression. There is only one trigger type: input_tokens, the default value is 150,000, and the minimum value that can be specified is 50,000. When the input token reaches this value, the API summarizes the conversation and creates a compaction block.
If set to true, you can stop immediately after summarizing, re-insert the most recent turn, and then continue. If false, it continues immediately without stopping.

Giving instructions completely replaces the default summary prompt rather than supplementing it. When manually specifying what to preserve, be sure to include everything you need. If left blank, the default prompt for each model will be used.

screens.outro: In requests after compression, the API discards the content before the compaction block and continues from the summary. Below are the settings for other services.

screens.outro: Now that we've seen compression, let's check step-by-step how to erase without summarizing.

screens.title: Prompt Cache: Reuse only if the first part is the same.
screens.lead: Select the right arrow to walk through step-by-step how Prompt Cache works. The last step links to why the cache is problematic when clearing the tool results.

visual.alt: A two-line diagram where if the first part of the request is the same, the cache is read, and if the middle part is cleared, the second part is recalculated.

steps.title: The request is sent again from the beginning every time
steps.body: The Model API does not remember previous requests. Each time the agent makes another call, it sends back the tool definition, system instructions, all previous conversations and tool results, and the model processes these input tokens from the beginning. The longer the conversation, the heavier each call becomes.

steps.title: The cache remembers the results of previous processing.
steps.body: Prompt cache is a function that stores the results of processing the first part of a request for a certain period of time and reuses them without recalculating them if the first part of the next request is the same. The order in which the cache looks is tool definition, system instruction, and message order. It fits well into agent loops where the same instructions and the same conversation history are repeated.

steps.title: The only thing that is reused is the prefix
steps.body: Reuse only occurs in prefixes that continue from the beginning without differing a single letter. To compare it to a book, if the first 100 pages are the same, that part is written as is, but if one line on page 50 is changed, everything after page 50 must be read anew. If the first part changes, the cache cannot be used even if the content behind it is the same.

steps.title: Reading is cheap, writing is a bit expensive
steps.body: Input tokens read from the cache are computed at a much lower cost than regular input, and response preparation is also faster by skipping parts that have already been processed. Conversely, when writing to the cache for the first time, a higher unit price is charged than a normal input. The default retention time is 5 minutes, and the retention time is updated each time the cache is used. The more often you reuse the same prefix, the greater the benefit.

steps.title: If you delete the middle part, everything after it becomes invalid.
steps.body: If you clear intermediate tool results with a context edit, the prefix of the request will change from the point you cleared. Anything before the deleted point will continue to be reused, but anything after it will become a new prefix and must be reprocessed and written to the cache again on the next request. Clearing reduces input tokens, but at the same time incurs the cost of one cache write.

steps.title: So I collect them and erase them in a big way.
steps.body: If you erase little by little often, the cache will be rewritten each time you erase, and the cost of rewriting may be greater than the tokens saved. So, set the threshold high enough, set a minimum amount to erase each time, and only execute when it is worth erasing. After clearing, the new prefix is ​​placed in the cache, so subsequent requests return to the per-read price.

steps.title: What is a thinking block
steps.body: A thinking block is a block of reasoning left behind by the model before it provides an answer when extended thinking is turned on. Leaving a thinking block from a previous turn preserves the cache, while clearing it invalidates the cache at the point where you cleared it. So, how much thinking is left is a setting that chooses between cache performance and context availability.

screens.outro: Now that you understand the principle, let's read the settings that determine when and how much of the tool's results are cleared.

screens.title: Edit context: remove tool results and clean up thinking
screens.lead: Read the settings below to determine when and how much of the tool's results are cleared.

notes.note: The clear_tool_uses_20250919 strategy clears tool results in chronological order, starting with the oldest when the context exceeds a threshold. The default trigger in the document is 100,000 input tokens, and 30,000 is used as an example here. By default, it only clears the tool results.

keep is the number of recent tool uses to keep even after clearing. The default is 3, but if you set it too small, even the results you just wrote will be lost, causing the agent to call the same tool again.

clear_at_least is the minimum number of tokens to clear in one clear. Clearing it invalidates the prompt cache at that point, offsetting the cost of rebuilding the cache by ensuring it only runs when it's worth clearing.
It does not clear the results of tools you put in exclude_tools. Used to protect search results that need to be constantly referenced. To clear even tool call inputs, set clear_tool_inputs to true.

screens.outro: The clear_thinking_20251015 strategy for organizing thinking blocks determines how many turns of thinking from the previous assistant turn will remain. Now let's move on to the case.

screens.title: Explanatory example: When the threshold is set too low
screens.lead: The instructor explains the case step by step. Select the right arrow to proceed to the next step.

steps.title: situation
steps.body: Set the code migration agent's compression threshold to a low value. Even a small increase in input tokens triggers a digest, repeating the digest multiple times during the operation. On the face of it, the input token is always light, which seems cost-effective.

steps.title: Step 1: Details are reduced to one line
steps.body: As the summary is repeated, the details of architectural decisions or yet-to-be-solved bugs are reduced to a single line. Losses are cumulative because summaries recapitulate previous summaries.

steps.title: Step 2: Ask the same question again
steps.body: Details that become important dozens of turns later are already left out of the summary. The agent repeats the same questions without knowing the decision has already been made, or touches on areas that have already been corrected.

steps.title: Stage 3: The basis for recent decisions becomes unclear
steps.body: If you repeat the summary, even the most recent turns will not remain in the original text, blurring the basis for the decisions you just made. As a result, the agent becomes less consistent.

steps.title: Why isn't it noticeable?
steps.body: What makes this problem difficult is that symptoms appear late. Immediately after the summary runs, the response seems fine, and only when the missing details are needed does the agent ask the wrong questions. Therefore, it is easy to blame the model rather than finding the cause in the summary settings. Looking only at cost indicators, the lower the threshold appears to be better, which also increases misunderstanding.

steps.title: improvement
steps.body: Raise the threshold and set it to preserve recent events in their original text. In ADK, event_retention_size plays that role. The summary instructions state that decisions are made and issues are left unresolved. In Claude, you can write your own summary prompts with instructions, but keep in mind that they completely replace the default prompts, so make sure to include any necessary preserves. After making improvements, run the same task again to see if the agent is asking the same questions again.

screens.outro: Let's also balance the issues with high thresholds.

screens.title: Illustrative Example: Quality and Cost by Threshold
screens.lead: Move the slider to see how quality and cost change as you change the threshold.

stops.body: Input tokens are light, but frequently summarized, resulting in high risk of loss of detail. In tasks where decision history is important, symptoms may appear such as repeating the same questions or reversing previous decisions.
Some of the original text remains, and summaries are executed at appropriate times. It's a good starting point for most tasks. The document defaults to 150,000 input tokens and the minimum is 50,000.

The original text remains for a long time and is precise, but the input is long, resulting in high costs and delays. High is not always safe, as longer contexts can also lead to context corrosion, which degrades quality.

If you have a majority of tool results, removing tool results is a less costly first resort than summarizing. If the decision history is important, compress it, but specify what to preserve in your summary instructions. The best value is not fixed but depends on the nature of the task, i.e. the weight of the tool's results and the importance of the decision.

No matter what value you choose, you need to confirm it after setting it. Let's run the same task again to see that after the summary, the agent doesn't re-ask for decisions it has already made and doesn't re-invoke cleared tool results. If you're calling the same tool repeatedly, it's a sign that your keep or threshold is too aggressive. Conversely, if the response is slow and the cost is high, the threshold is too high. In this way, the value is adjusted backwards from the symptom.

Editing and compression are not mutually exclusive. You can do this by first reducing the volume by removing tool results, and then compressing the window when it's still full, thus summarizing the entire conversation. This delays the need for summarization, reduces loss of detail, and makes the summary object itself lighter. Since the threshold for each stage must be set differently, it is natural to set the trigger for removal lower than the trigger for compression.

items.prompt: Replace Compression with Summary and Clear Context Edit with Rules
items.answer: Compression replaces old turns with model-written summaries, and context editing rules out tool results or thinking blocks without summaries. Placeholder text remains where you erase it so the model can tell. Edits are applied on the server and the original conversation history on the client remains intact.

items.prompt: Compression threshold is a key setting that separates quality and cost.
items.answer: If it is low, there will be frequent summarization, resulting in a large loss of detail; if it is high, the input will be long, resulting in high cost and delay. The optimal value depends on the nature of the task, and changing the value ensures that the agent does not re-ask for decisions it has already made.

items.prompt: Removing tool results is the least damaging first resort.
items.answer: If most of the tool results have already been processed, removal causes less information loss than summarization. However, clearing invalidates the prompt cache at the point where it was cleared, so only run it when it is worth clearing with clear_at_least.

items.prompt: ADK and OpenAI also compress using the same principle of using threshold and recency preservation.
items.answer: ADK uses token_threshold and event_retention_size, and OpenAI uses compact_threshold and compaction items. Although the names are different, the principle is the same: when the threshold is reached, it is summarized and the most recent content is left. Even if you move services, your design judgments remain the same.

screens.outro: Lastly, let's think about it in relation to our own work.

screens.title: Connect to my work
screens.lead: This screen is for reading only. Read the questions and think for yourself. You will not enter or submit an answer.

paragraphs: Key terms in this lesson are Compaction, compression threshold, context editing, and tool result removal. Think about which tool results your agent accumulates the most, and how often you need those results again.

If your task has a lot of tool output, you might consider eliminating it first. If your task involves a lot of tool results, you might consider how to write summary instructions. The two methods can be used together, and you need to make sure that the agent doesn't repeat the same questions after reducing either method. If you just set a value without checking, problems will appear much later.

There is always a cost to cutting back. Compression can lose detail, and stripping can invalidate the cache. The design discussed in this class is comparing the costs and benefits to determine the threshold and conservation range.

To summarize, the order of inspection is as follows. First, we see what the majority of the context is. Second, get rid of anything you don't need again. Third, summarize what needs to be meaningful and specify the items to be preserved. Fourth, the most recent content is left in the original text. These four are the basic framework for compression and editing settings.

callout.label: Questions to Think About
callout.text: Where does Compaction stand in the way of my work? Even if you summarize, think together about what information you cannot afford to lose and what information you can delete.

checks.q: What happens if I specify the instructions value directly in the compaction settings?
options: Used in addition to the default summary prompt.
You can now pause immediately after the summary and re-enter your most recent turn.
Completely replaces the default summary prompt
Changes the input token threshold at which compression occurs
checks.explain: The instructions do not supplement the default summary prompt, but completely replace it. Therefore, when directly specifying items to preserve, be sure to include all necessary information.

wrong.1: Pausing immediately after summary is the role of pause_after_compaction.
wrong.3: The threshold is determined by separate trigger settings.

checks.intro: Check out how Compaction's instructions settings are related to the default operation.
checks.correctFeedback: That's right. Specifying instructions completely replaces the default summary prompt rather than supplementing it.
checks.incorrectFeedback: It's easy to think that it's added, but it's not. Remember that only the values ​​you specify will be used, so you must write down all items to be preserved.

checks.q: What happens to the prompt cache when you clear tool results in mid-context?
options: The cache is always intact so there is no impact on costs.
The area before the deleted point continues to be reused, but the area behind it is processed anew and written back to the cache.
The entire cache is deleted and the cache cannot be reused later.
The cache compares only the last line, so deleting the middle has no effect.
checks.explain: The cache only reuses prefixes that continue the same way from the beginning. If you erase the middle, the part after that point becomes a new prefix and will be processed and recorded again, so it is advantageous to erase it by gathering enough to be worth erasing.

wrong.0: Because the prefix changes, the cache behind the erased point cannot be used, and new recording costs are incurred.
wrong.2: The front prefix remains the same, so the area before the deleted point continues to be reused. The new prefix is ​​also written back to the cache.
wrong.3: The cache checks whether all prefixes from the beginning, not just the last line, are the same.

checks.intro: Check out for yourself the principles of the cache you just saw. Results are not recorded.
checks.correctFeedback: That's right. The principle is that the front part with the same prefix is ​​reused, and the part behind the changed point is processed and recorded again.
checks.incorrectFeedback: The cache only reuses prefixes that continue identically from the previous one. If the middle changes, reconsider which parts are reused and which parts are recalculated.

checks.q: Match the following settings or concepts with their roles:
right: Allows you to stop immediately after the summary and reload the most recent turn.
Reduces cache invalidation loss by only executing when worth clearing
Reduce content by replacing old turns with model-written summaries
Clear old tool results according to rules without summarizing
checks.explain: Replace Compaction with Summary and clear Context Edit with Rule. pause_after_compaction and clear_at_least are auxiliary settings that deal with the side effects of both methods, respectively.
checks.intro: Pair compression and editing-related settings by role. It's okay if you don't get it right at once.
checks.correctFeedback: That's correct. You made a good distinction between the method of changing to summary and the method of deleting by rule, and the settings that deal with the side effects of each method.
checks.incorrectFeedback: There is a mismatched pair. Compaction is summary, context edit is removal of tool results, and pause_after_compaction and clear_at_least are auxiliary settings that cover the side effects of both methods respectively.

checks.q: Most of the coding agent's context is a result of the tools it has already processed, and its decision history is not very important. What is the best first resort with minimal losses?
options: Set the threshold very low to ensure that summarization runs frequently.
Raise the threshold as much as possible to retain the original text for a long time.
Have a client summarizer that handles the digest calls and record rewrites directly in your code.
Use context editing to clear old tool results with rules
checks.explain: If the majority of tool results are present, removing tool results is lighter and less costly than summarizing. When decision history is important, use condensation with summary instructions.

wrong.0: Frequent summaries reduce the details to a single line, increasing the risk of repeating the same questions.
wrong.1: The original text may remain for a long time, resulting in longer input times, resulting in costs, delays, and reduced quality.
wrong.2: It's possible, but you have to take charge of everything yourself, so it's not a light first option.

checks.intro: A coding agent where most of the context is the result of a tool. Choose the first option with the least amount of loss.
checks.correctFeedback: That's right. If decision history is not important, clearing older tool results rather than summaries is lighter and less costly.
checks.incorrectFeedback: The key is what fills the context. If the tool produces a large number of results, consider clearing them before replacing the information with a summary.

glossary.def: A way to reduce context by turning old conversations into model-written summaries.
Based on which compression is performed once the input token reaches this value. Lower runs more frequently and higher runs slower.
A way to clear specific content, such as tool results or thinking blocks, based on rules without summarizing.
The clear_tool_uses strategy replaces old tool results with placeholder text.
An opaque item returned by OpenAI's server-side compression, which compresses and passes the previous state to the next window.

This is a function that stores the results of processing the first part of the request and reuses them when the first part of the next request is the same. Only the prefixes that start from the beginning are reused, so if you change the middle, the ones that come after are processed anew.

misconceptions.fact: The summary is at a loss. Lower thresholds mean that more frequent summarization reduces detail and accumulates loss.

misconceptions.myth: Context editing and compression are the same thing.
misconceptions.fact: Edit clears the rule without summary, and Compress replaces it with a summary. The majority of tool results make editing lighter and less lossy.

misconceptions.myth: Even if you delete the content, the cost is reduced and there are no side effects.
misconceptions.fact: Clearing the tool results invalidates the prompt cache at that point. clear_at_least should only be executed when it is worth clearing.

closing.lead: Summarizes the key points of this class.
points: Replace compression with summary and clear context editing with rules.
Compression threshold is a key setting that makes the difference between quality and cost.
Removing tool results is the least damaging first resort.
ADK and OpenAI also compress using the same principle of using threshold and recency preservation.
closing.reflectionLead: This is a question to think about for yourself. It will not be submitted or graded.
closing.reflection: Where does Compaction stand in the way of my work?
